title: Tzav: ear, thumb, toe (Leviticus 8:23–24)
hook: priests are anointed on the ear, the thumb and the big toe: hear, do, walk
tomorrow: Tzav: seven days at the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, todah, the thanks offering brought after a rescue. Your line was thanks outlasts everything. Whose rescue story did you tell? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

If you were designing a ceremony to make someone a priest, where would you put the mark? The forehead, maybe, like a crown. The heart. The hands, which will do the work. The Torah picks three places nobody would guess. Not the head. Not the chest. The edge of the right ear. The thumb of the right hand. And the big toe of the right foot. It sounds almost comic until you stop and ask what those three have in common, and what they leave out.
screen: `WHERE WOULD YOU PUT THE MARK?` → `NOT THE HEAD, NOT THE HEART.` → `EAR, THUMB, BIG TOE.`

segments.voice: It's the week of the priests' ordination. Moses, acting as priest himself for these days, brings a ram called the ram of consecration, and takes some of its blood. The text, in the JPS 1917 translation, says he put it "upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot." Then he does the same for each of Aaron's sons. The Torah doesn't explain the choice. It simply describes it. Many commentators over the centuries have read it as a map of a life of service. The ear, to listen: to God, and to the people who come with their troubles. The hand, to do the work. The foot, to walk in the right path, and to go where you're needed. Listening first, then doing, then walking. And notice the order runs from top to bottom: the whole body, claimed for service, from ear to toe. Here's a surprise from later in Leviticus. The exact same marking, ear, thumb and toe, is done for someone else: a person healed from the skin affliction called tzara'at, who had been living outside the camp and is now coming home. The priest, starting his service, and the outcast, returning to the community, receive the same three touches. Whatever it means, it isn't about rank. It's about a person beginning again, with ears, hands and feet given a new purpose.
screen: `THE RAM OF CONSECRATION.` · `EAR, THUMB AND BIG TOE.` · `LISTEN, THEN DO, THEN WALK.` · `THE SAME MARK FOR ONE RETURNING.` · then, large: `LISTEN, DO, WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your ears, hands and feet. Settle, and breathe. Touch your right ear gently. Ask: what do I need to listen for today, and who needs me to listen? Then touch your right thumb. Ask: what's one thing my hands should do today? Then press your right big toe to the floor. Ask: where do I need to go, or not go? Take a breath with each. Then sit with all three, ear, hand and foot, ready. The bell holds the time.
Tzav. Command. The portion where the priests are ordained, marked on the right ear, the right thumb and the right big toe.
Your line: listen, do, walk. Today, before one conversation, touch your ear, and listen fully before you act. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

screen: `DAY 388 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TZAV: SEVEN DAYS AT THE DOOR.`

howItsDone: The ordination ceremony of Leviticus 8 is read in the portion Tzav, and the same ear, thumb and toe rite appears in Leviticus 14 for a person healed of tzara'at.

fork.setup: Moses is ordaining Aaron with the blood of the ram of consecration. where does he put it?
options: on the forehead and the heart.
on the right ear, right thumb and right big toe.
fork.reveal: upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and the great toe of his right foot. many read it as listen, do, walk.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange ancient ritual.
what it means: the priest's whole body, from ear to toe, is given to service: listening, doing, walking.
what a scholar hears: the same rite on ear, thumb and toe is used for the healed metzora (Leviticus 14:14), linking the priest's beginning with an outsider's return.
